newsitem.title: USA: Archer seeks mild cut, then ethanol tax break end.
newsitem.headline: Archer seeks mild cut, then ethanol tax break end.

text.p: The tax package unveiled Monday by U.S. House tax chairman Bill Archer asked a slight reduction -- 0.3 cent per gallon -- in the 5.4 cent fuel-tax break for ethanol and elimination of the break in 2000.

Documents released by Archer's office also proposed a penalty on "excess" ethanol production while the 5.1 cent tax break was in effect, an increase in tax credits allowed for small ethanol producers, within limits, and immediate repeal of subsidies for ETBE, a competitor fuel.
Archer, R-Texas, said at a news conference that the ethanol tax break diverted corn to an artificial, industrial use at the same time the world needed more food.
"If there were ever an anachronistic provision in the tax code, it is this one," Archer said.
"It makes absolutely no sense. It should be removed."

Farm-state lawmakers and ethanol backers had expected Archer would seek an outright end to preferential treatment for the home-grown fuel. Such a step would kill 120,000 jobs and billions of dollars a year in income for farmers and grain processors.
Reprsentative Jim Nussle, Iowa Republican, said he would file an amendment on Wednesday to checkmate Archer on ethanol.
Analyst John Urbanchuk, of AUS Consultants, said by going slow on ethanol now, Archer was aiming at ending the tax break at decade's end, when it is now scheduled to expire.
"Probably, politically it is setting the stage for elimination in the year 2000," Urbanchuck told Reuters.
Asked if his proposal on ethanol would be supported by lawmakers, Archer replied, "We think this is totally sustainable. We're going to pursue it."
Archer said his package would limit use of the ethanol producer tax credit to plants already in operation.
It would increase the producer tax credit, now 10 cents per gallon, to 13 cents but limit its application to a producer's average production during 1993-97.

Overall, Archer's proposals on ethanol would bring the government an additional $4.1 billion over the next decade. Relatively small amounts would come from shaving the fuel-tax break -- less than $100 million a year -- but gains would approach $600 million a year when the break was eliminated.
"Any modification of the current ethanol tax credit is unacceptable," Nussle told a news conference.
He said it was not clear yet whether ethanol backers had the votes in committee to beat Archer. He also said he did not expect any help from the House leadership unlike years past.
"The discussions with the leadership have been positive but we understand that at a least for the time being we're on our own and we will do battle accordingly," Nussle said. rueter
